title: Contraception: Match the Method to Risk
bottomLine: Contraceptive counseling should be person-centered and noncoercive. Safety depends on the method and the patient's conditions; estrogen-containing methods require particular attention to thrombotic/cardiovascular risk, while IUDs and implants provide highly effective reversible contraception but do not protect against STIs.
recognize: Smoking at older age, migraine with aura, prior VTE/thrombophilia, severe hypertension, and certain postpartum periods can make estrogen-containing contraception unsafe or less appropriate.
Long-acting reversible contraception can be used by adolescents and patients who have not given birth when otherwise medically eligible.
priorities: Assess pregnancy possibility, medical history, medications, BP when relevant, reproductive goals, STI risk, and patient preference.
Use current U.S. MEC/SPR rather than memorized blanket exclusions.
Counsel that condoms reduce STI risk even when another contraceptive method is used.
assessMonitor: Monitor method satisfaction, bleeding concerns, BP for combined hormonal methods, new health conditions, and medication interactions.
interventions: Provide clear missed-dose/late-dose instructions for the chosen method using current product/CDC guidance.
Remove unnecessary barriers to method initiation when pregnancy can reasonably be excluded.
medicationSafety: Enzyme-inducing medications can reduce effectiveness of some hormonal methods.
Combined hormonal contraception is not appropriate for every migraine, smoking, hypertension, or clot-risk profile; use category-specific guidance.
teaching: No contraceptive method except barrier methods used correctly reduces STI exposure risk; discuss dual protection when appropriate.
delegationScope: Contraceptive eligibility assessment and prescribing are role/state specific; the PN reinforces teaching and reports contraindication clues within scope.
examTrap: Assuming an IUD is contraindicated solely because the patient is an adolescent or has never given birth.
oneLinePearl: Contraception is preference + eligibility + STI prevention—not one-size-fits-all.
sourceBasis: CDC U.S. Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use 2024
CDC U.S. Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use 2024

title: Emergency Contraception
bottomLine: Emergency contraception prevents pregnancy after unprotected intercourse or contraceptive failure; it does not terminate an established pregnancy. Options include a copper IUD and emergency contraceptive pills, with effectiveness and follow-up depending on method and timing.
recognize: The copper IUD is the most effective emergency-contraception option when medically eligible and can provide ongoing contraception.
Ulipristal and levonorgestrel emergency contraceptive pills have different instructions for restarting hormonal contraception.
priorities: Determine timing of intercourse, pregnancy possibility, current contraception, medications, and patient preference.
Provide the method as soon as feasible according to current guidance.
Explain when backup contraception and pregnancy testing are needed.
assessMonitor: Assess for delayed menses, pregnancy symptoms, severe abdominal pain, and ongoing contraceptive needs.
interventions: Offer ongoing contraception and STI testing/prevention based on risk and patient goals.
medicationSafety: After ulipristal, starting progestin-containing hormonal contraception too soon can reduce ulipristal effectiveness; follow current CDC timing guidance.
Drug interactions with enzyme inducers can reduce effectiveness of some emergency contraceptive pills.
complications: Delayed recognition of ectopic pregnancy if pregnancy occurs
redFlags: Heavy bleeding with positive pregnancy test
teaching: Emergency contraception does not protect against future intercourse unless the chosen ongoing method is active.
delegationScope: Counseling and access laws for minors vary by state; follow local policy while preserving confidentiality as legally permitted.
examTrap: Telling a patient that emergency contraception causes abortion.
oneLinePearl: Emergency contraception prevents pregnancy; it does not end an implanted pregnancy.
sourceBasis: CDC U.S. Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use 2024

title: Chlamydia: Treat the Patient and Prevent Reinfection
bottomLine: Chlamydia is often asymptomatic but can cause PID, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and neonatal infection. Treat promptly, address sex partners, test for other STIs, and retest after treatment because reinfection is common.
recognize: Cervicitis, urethritis, dysuria, discharge, postcoital bleeding, pelvic pain, or epididymal pain may occur, but many infections have no symptoms.
Pregnancy changes the recommended antibiotic regimen and follow-up.
priorities: Collect appropriate NAAT testing when indicated and start treatment promptly when diagnosed/presumptively treated.
Teach abstinence from sexual activity until the treatment interval is complete and partners have been treated according to CDC guidance.
Arrange retesting around 3 months after treatment.
assessMonitor: Assess pelvic pain/fever for PID, pregnancy status, adherence, partner treatment, and persistent symptoms.
interventions: Offer HIV, gonorrhea, and syphilis testing per CDC guidance.
Use expedited partner therapy where legal and clinically appropriate according to state rules.
medicationSafety: Doxycycline is preferred for many nonpregnant adolescent/adult infections; pregnancy uses a different regimen under current CDC guidance.
Avoid assuming azithromycin is always equivalent across infection sites.
redFlags: Pregnancy with pelvic pain or bleeding
teaching: Feeling better does not mean partners are treated; reinfection is common without partner management.
delegationScope: STI counseling, treatment, and minor-consent rules vary by state; preserve confidentiality within law and policy.
examTrap: Treating the patient but ignoring partner treatment and retesting.
oneLinePearl: Chlamydia care is treatment + partners + retest.
sourceBasis: CDC STI Treatment Guidelines: Chlamydial Infections

title: Gonorrhea: Resistance Makes Follow-Up Matter
bottomLine: Gonorrhea can be asymptomatic and can cause PID, infertility, disseminated infection, and neonatal disease. Current U.S. therapy is ceftriaxone-based for uncomplicated infection, with chlamydia treatment added when chlamydia has not been excluded; pharyngeal infection requires special follow-up.
recognize: Urethral/cervical discharge, dysuria, pelvic pain, rectal symptoms, or pharyngeal infection may occur.
Disseminated gonococcal infection can present with fever, migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, dermatitis, or septic arthritis.
priorities: Treat promptly with the current CDC regimen.
Assess site of exposure so appropriate anatomic sites are tested.
Address sex partners and test for chlamydia, syphilis, and HIV.
assessMonitor: Assess persistent symptoms, adherence, partner treatment, pregnancy, and possible treatment failure versus reinfection.
interventions: Pharyngeal gonorrhea requires a test of cure according to CDC guidance.
Suspected treatment failure requires culture/susceptibility evaluation and public-health consultation/reporting pathways.
medicationSafety: Severe cephalosporin allergy requires expert alternative-regimen guidance, especially for pharyngeal infection.
teaching: Avoid sexual activity for the CDC-specified period after treatment and until partners are treated.
delegationScope: Partner therapy and reporting rules can vary by state; follow local public-health law/policy.
examTrap: Assuming a negative urine test rules out pharyngeal or rectal infection after exposure at those sites.
oneLinePearl: Test the exposed site, treat with current CDC therapy, manage partners.
sourceBasis: CDC STI Treatment Guidelines: Gonococcal Infections Among Adolescents and Adults

title: Syphilis: Stage Determines Treatment
bottomLine: Syphilis is systemic and staged; treatment regimen depends on stage and neurologic/ocular involvement. Penicillin G is the preferred therapy across stages, and penicillin is the only therapy with documented efficacy for syphilis during pregnancy.
recognize: Primary syphilis may cause a painless chancre; secondary disease can cause rash including palms/soles, mucous lesions, lymphadenopathy, or systemic symptoms.
Latent infection has positive serology without symptoms; neurologic, ocular, or otic disease can occur at various stages.
priorities: Clarify stage, pregnancy status, neurologic/ocular/otic symptoms, and HIV status.
Use the correct penicillin formulation for the indication; Bicillin C-R is not an appropriate substitute for Bicillin L-A in syphilis treatment.
Coordinate partner notification and public-health follow-up.
assessMonitor: Trend symptoms and quantitative nontreponemal titers at recommended intervals.
Assess for Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction after treatment.
interventions: Pregnant patients with penicillin allergy require desensitization and penicillin treatment rather than substitution with an unproven regimen.
medicationSafety: The penicillin preparation, dose, and duration depend on stage and CNS/ocular involvement.
A Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is an inflammatory response after treatment and is not itself a penicillin allergy.
teaching: Partner evaluation and follow-up blood testing are essential even after symptoms resolve.
delegationScope: Syphilis reporting and partner-service requirements involve public health and vary procedurally by jurisdiction.
examTrap: Using the wrong long-acting penicillin combination product because the brand names look similar.
oneLinePearl: Syphilis treatment is stage-specific—and pregnancy still means penicillin.

title: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease
bottomLine: PID is an upper-genital-tract infection that can threaten fertility even when symptoms are mild. Lower abdominal/pelvic pain with cervical motion, uterine, or adnexal tenderness can justify empiric treatment when no better diagnosis explains the presentation.
recognize: Abnormal discharge, fever, dyspareunia, irregular bleeding, and dysuria may accompany pelvic pain.
A negative cervical gonorrhea/chlamydia test does not exclude upper-tract PID.
priorities: Assess pregnancy status because ectopic pregnancy is a critical alternative diagnosis.
Start prescribed broad-spectrum treatment promptly when PID is suspected.
Assess whether hospitalization criteria or tubo-ovarian abscess concern is present.
assessMonitor: Trend fever, pain, tenderness, vomiting, adherence, partner treatment, and response within the expected follow-up interval.
interventions: Test for gonorrhea, chlamydia, HIV, and syphilis as indicated and arrange partner treatment.
Reevaluate if symptoms fail to improve promptly.
medicationSafety: Complete the full multi-drug regimen even if symptoms improve early.
Pregnancy requires specialist management/hospital evaluation because standard outpatient regimens may not apply.
teaching: Abstain from sexual activity until treatment is complete, symptoms resolve, and partners are treated per CDC guidance.
delegationScope: New pelvic pain and pregnancy-risk assessment require licensed-nurse/provider evaluation.
examTrap: Waiting for a positive gonorrhea/chlamydia test before treating a classic PID presentation.
oneLinePearl: PID is treated early to protect future fertility.
sourceBasis: CDC STI Treatment Guidelines: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease

title: Ectopic Pregnancy: Pain, Bleeding, Shock
bottomLine: Any reproductive-age patient with possible pregnancy plus pelvic/abdominal pain or vaginal bleeding needs ectopic pregnancy considered. Rupture can cause life-threatening internal hemorrhage with shoulder pain, syncope, hypotension, tachycardia, or peritoneal signs.
recognize: Pain may be unilateral or diffuse and bleeding can be light despite major internal blood loss.
Risk rises with prior ectopic pregnancy, tubal surgery/disease, or pregnancy with an IUD in place, but ectopic pregnancy can occur without known risk factors.
priorities: Check pregnancy status promptly.
Assess hemodynamics, pain, bleeding, shoulder pain, syncope, and peritoneal findings.
Escalate instability immediately for emergency surgical evaluation/resuscitation.
assessMonitor: Trend vital signs, mental status, pain, hemoglobin when ordered, serial hCG, and ultrasound findings through the care plan.
interventions: Maintain IV access and prepare for blood products/surgery if rupture is suspected.
Stable patients may be managed medically or surgically depending on criteria.
medicationSafety: Methotrexate management requires strict eligibility, follow-up hCG monitoring, and avoidance of contraindicated substances/medications per protocol.
teaching: After medical management, follow hCG until resolved and seek emergency care for worsening pain, dizziness, or heavy bleeding.
delegationScope: Possible ruptured ectopic pregnancy requires immediate licensed clinical assessment and escalation.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient because vaginal bleeding is light even though shock symptoms are developing.
oneLinePearl: Light vaginal bleeding does not mean light internal bleeding.

title: HPV Vaccination and Cancer Prevention
bottomLine: HPV vaccination prevents infections that cause multiple cancers and works best before exposure. Follow the current CDC immunization schedule for routine, catch-up, and shared-decision age groups; vaccination does not replace indicated cervical cancer screening.
recognize: Dose number and interval depend on age at series initiation and immune status.
Prior sexual activity or known HPV exposure does not automatically remove all potential vaccine benefit.
priorities: Check vaccine history and age/immune status.
Use current CDC schedule rather than restarting a delayed series.
Observe standard vaccine contraindications and syncope precautions.
assessMonitor: Monitor for immediate allergic reaction and vasovagal syncope after vaccination.
interventions: Administer catch-up doses without restarting the series when intervals are longer than recommended.
medicationSafety: Severe allergic reaction to a prior dose/component is a contraindication; pregnancy generally leads to delaying remaining HPV doses until after pregnancy rather than intervention for inadvertent vaccination.
complications: Vaccine-preventable HPV-related cancers and precancers when underimmunized
teaching: HPV vaccination is cancer prevention; screening may still be needed later according to cervical screening guidance.
delegationScope: Vaccine administration follows state/facility scope and standing-order policy.
examTrap: Restarting the entire HPV vaccine series because a dose was late.
oneLinePearl: Late vaccine dose? Continue the series—do not restart.
sourceBasis: CDC Immunization Schedule currently in force

title: Cervical Cancer Screening
bottomLine: Cervical cancer screening intervals depend on age, test type, cervix status, prior results, and high-risk conditions. Do not screen simply because sexual activity began early, and do not apply routine-risk intervals to patients with prior high-grade lesions, immunocompromise, or other special risk.
recognize: The current final USPSTF recommendation remains the 2018 statement while an updated recommendation is in progress as of 2026.
Routine screening is not recommended under age 21 regardless of sexual history under the current final USPSTF recommendation.
priorities: Confirm age, whether the cervix is present, prior screening results, high-grade lesion/cancer history, HIV/immunocompromise, and DES exposure history when relevant.
Use the current final national guideline and local system protocol because screening recommendations are actively evolving.
assessMonitor: Track whether abnormal results receive appropriate diagnostic follow-up; screening is only effective when abnormal findings are closed-loop managed.
interventions: Educate on HPV vaccination and screening as complementary prevention strategies.
teaching: A Pap/HPV screening test is preventive care, not a diagnostic test for new concerning symptoms; symptoms need clinical evaluation.
delegationScope: Screening collection scope varies by state/setting; abnormal-result counseling and follow-up require licensed clinical management.
examTrap: Screening a healthy 19-year-old solely because they are sexually active.
oneLinePearl: Screen by guideline and risk—not by sexual activity alone.
sourceBasis: USPSTF Final Recommendation: Cervical Cancer Screening 2018, update in progress as of 2026
ACOG cervical cancer screening practice advisory

title: Sexual Assault: Trauma-Informed Immediate Care
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: After sexual assault, immediate priorities are medical stabilization, privacy, consent for each part of care, trauma-informed communication, time-sensitive pregnancy/STI/HIV prevention options, and access to a trained forensic examiner when desired/available. Evidence collection should never override urgent medical needs or patient autonomy.
recognize: Patients may present immediately or days later and may have no visible injuries.
Fragmented recall, flat affect, or delayed reporting can occur after trauma and do not prove or disprove assault.
priorities: Treat life-threatening injuries first.
Explain choices and obtain consent separately for medical treatment, forensic examination, photography, and evidence collection as required.
Preserve evidence only within the patient's choices and legal requirements.
assessMonitor: Assess safety, injuries, strangulation symptoms, pregnancy risk, STI/HIV exposure risk, substance-facilitated assault concern, suicide risk, and safe discharge resources.
interventions: Offer emergency contraception, STI prophylaxis/testing, hepatitis B vaccination, and HIV PEP evaluation when indicated and within time windows.
Connect with sexual-assault advocacy and follow-up care.
medicationSafety: HIV PEP is time-sensitive and should be initiated promptly when indicated rather than delayed for all test results.
teaching: The patient controls choices about examination and support within applicable legal requirements; offer written follow-up and crisis resources.
delegationScope: Mandatory reporting, forensic consent, and minor/adult reporting rules vary by state; follow law and trained forensic protocols.
examTrap: Pressuring the patient to shower, change clothes, or complete a forensic exam before discussing choices and consent.
oneLinePearl: Safety and consent first; evidence collection never outranks the patient.
sourceBasis: U.S. DOJ National Protocol for Sexual Assault Medical Forensic Examinations
CDC STI Treatment Guidelines: Sexual Assault

title: Intimate Partner Violence: Ask Privately, Plan Safely
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Suspected intimate partner violence should be assessed privately, without the partner or family serving as interpreter. Validate concerns, assess immediate danger and strangulation/weapons/escalation risk, document objectively, and offer individualized safety resources without forcing a patient to leave before they are ready unless mandatory protections apply.
recognize: Repeated injuries, delayed care, controlling partner behavior, reproductive coercion, strangulation history, or inconsistent explanations can raise concern.
Leaving an abusive relationship can temporarily increase danger, so simplistic advice to 'just leave' can be unsafe.
priorities: Interview alone using a qualified interpreter when needed.
Assess immediate danger, threats to children/dependents, weapons, strangulation, stalking, and escalation.
Create a discreet safety plan and connect with advocacy resources.
assessMonitor: Document injuries and patient statements objectively, assess pregnancy, mental health/suicide risk, and safe methods of follow-up/contact.
interventions: Offer resources in a way that does not increase danger if the abusive partner monitors phone, email, or belongings.
teaching: Help is available; decisions about leaving should be supported through a safety-focused plan rather than coercion.
delegationScope: Reporting duties vary by state, age, injury type, and vulnerable-adult/child status; know the local law and facility policy.
examTrap: Using the suspected abusive partner as the interpreter for screening questions.
oneLinePearl: Ask alone, assess danger, document facts, support—not coerce.
sourceBasis: Futures Without Violence healthcare IPV resources
USPSTF intimate partner violence screening recommendation
